subject: history
title: Total War 1939-45
welcome_lead: Barbarossa, Holocaust and Hiroshima: the conflict's defining moments.
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on Operation Barbarossa, the Holocaust and the end of WWII.
final_note: You have stood on the rubble of 1945.

concepts.def: Combined-arms warfare pairing armour, infantry and tactical aircraft, demonstrated in France May-June 1940.
German invasion of the USSR launched on 22 June 1941 with 3 million troops along a 1,800-mile front.
Meeting on 20 January 1942 coordinating the Final Solution, the systematic murder of European Jewry.
Soviet victory in February 1943 capturing the German Sixth Army, marking the eastern front turning point.
Allied invasion of Normandy on 6 June 1944 with 156,000 troops landed on five beaches.
First atomic bomb dropped on 6 August 1945, killing approximately 80,000 immediately; Nagasaki followed on 9 August.

walkthroughs.body_html: Hitler launched Operation Barbarossa on 22 June 1941 to destroy Bolshevism and seize Lebensraum. Initial encirclements captured 3 million Soviets; the offensive stalled before Moscow in December. Soviet recovery, US Lend-Lease and German overextension produced victory at Stalingrad in February 1943 and Kursk in July 1943. By 1945 the Red Army had reached Berlin, taking enormous Soviet casualties of c. 27 million.

Persecution escalated from the 1935 Nuremberg Laws and 1938 Kristallnacht to systematic mass murder. Einsatzgruppen killed about 1.5 million Jews in the USSR from 1941. The Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942 coordinated industrial murder; six death camps including Auschwitz-Birkenau killed approximately 6 million Jews. Historiographical debate persists between intentionalist and functionalist explanations.

After Okinawa (April-June 1945) inflicted heavy US casualties, planners feared a 1946 invasion of Japan would cost a million lives. Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, plus Soviet entry on 8 August, prompted Hirohito's surrender broadcast on 15 August. Gar Alperovitz argued the bombs were dropped chiefly to intimidate the USSR; mainstream historians cite mixed military and political motives.
